title: Wikimedia asks court to rule AI training fair use, but not chatbot copying
content:
The Wikimedia Foundation wants the judge in The New York Times’ copyright fight with OpenAI to split the question in two. Training an AI model on copyrighted work is likely fair use, it argues. A chatbot that copies websites to answer a user’s question is likely not.
The foundation runs Wikipedia. On Thursday, it asked the US District Court for the Southern District of New York for leave to file an amicus, or friend-of-the-court, brief. It announced the filing on Friday. The case, In re: OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation, combines 12 lawsuits against OpenAI, among them the Times’ 2023 suit against OpenAI and Microsoft.
Judge Sidney H. Stein will decide whether using copyrighted content to build large language models is fair use. That US legal doctrine allows some use of protected work without permission. He has not ruled on that, or on whether to accept the brief.
“We are taking a position in this case to defend the free and open human knowledge that Wikipedia depends on,” said Wikimedia Foundation chief executive Bernadette Meehan.
Training yes, chatbot answers no
The proposed Wikimedia amicus brief supports neither party. It says both sides push “overbroad and simplified” readings of fair use. The Times alleges that using its content for any purpose, including training, breaks copyright law. OpenAI and Microsoft say training on publicly available data is fair use, according to Wikimedia’s summary.
Wikimedia asks the court to judge each use separately, citing the Supreme Court’s 2023 Warhol ruling. Scraping a website is not itself a “use”, it argues. Only what a company does with the copies should count.
Training a general-purpose model is “likely to be fair”, the brief says. The model is something new, and it does not replace the works it learned from.
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is different. A chatbot using RAG copies text from sites such as Wikipedia or The New York Times when a user asks a question. It feeds the most relevant passages to the model and often reproduces much of the original in its answer, the brief says.
“While the pre-training of ChatGPT’s general LLM was fair use, OpenAI’s use of copies in ChatGPT’s RAG feature is not fair,” Wikimedia wrote in the brief.
Companies using RAG should follow each publisher’s licence terms, it argues. The same goes for newer techniques that serve a similar “grounding” purpose.
Credit and crawlers
For Wikipedia, that licence is Creative Commons CC BY-SA 4.0. It requires credit to the original authors, and adaptations must stay under the same licence. When chatbots use Wikipedia content without following those terms, people are steered away from contributing, Wikimedia told the court.
Scraping also strains its servers, the filing says. That pushes Wikimedia to add technical safeguards, which bad actors often get around. A public park can stay free and open while stopping someone from “driving a container truck through it”, one footnote says.
Wikimedia wants heavy users to follow its public rate limits or pay for its Enterprise service. This month, it said rogue OpenAI agents had edited its wikis without approval.
“Any conversation around fair use and copyright in the age of AI cannot be limited to for-profit organizations: it must include stakeholders across the entire online information ecosystem,” said Stephen LaPorte, the foundation’s general counsel.
The wider fight
Publishers have kept up the pressure on OpenAI. In June, nearly 400 local newspapers sued OpenAI and Microsoft. In July, the Times and other outlets asked a judge to sanction OpenAI, accusing it of hiding evidence. In September, the Justice Department sided with OpenAI, telling a New York court that AI training is fair use.
Wikipedia has more than 67 million articles in 300 languages, according to the foundation. Volunteers write it using reliable sources, including news articles.
“Expanding access to knowledge through AI is a powerful goal, but it must respect the people, contributors, and communities that make reliable knowledge possible,” Meehan said.

report.summary: 维基媒体吁法院区分AI训练与RAG复制
report.background: 维基媒体基金会向纽约南区法院申请提交法庭之友意见，介入《纽约时报》诉OpenAI等合并版权案。该案合并12起诉讼，核心是使用版权内容训练大模型是否属合理使用。此前出版商持续起诉OpenAI，美国司法部则支持AI训练属合理使用。维基百科内容按CC BY-SA 4.0开放，基金会担心AI scraping与未遵守许可会伤害贡献者生态。
key_points: 维基媒体不支持任何一方，认为双方对合理使用的解读都过于宽泛、简单化，主张法院按具体使用方式逐项判断。
用版权内容训练通用大模型“很可能属合理使用”，因为模型是新产品，不会替代其学习过的原作。
但RAG聊天机器人会在回答时复制并再现维基百科、《纽约时报》等网站段落，维基媒体认为这类使用不属合理使用。
使用RAG的公司应遵守各出版方许可条款；维基百科要求署名原作者，改编内容须继续按CC BY-SA相同许可开放。
大量抓取会加重服务器负担，维基媒体要求高频使用者遵守公开速率限制或购买Enterprise服务，并披露有OpenAI代理未经批准编辑其wiki。
report.impact: 对AI行业而言，合理使用不再是“一刀切”抗辩，训练与推理/RAG可能被分开审视。对开发者，RAG产品需更重视内容许可、署名、引用与速率限制，合规成本上升。对普通用户，AI答案可能更多显示来源与许可信息，部分内容访问方式或收费模式也可能变化。
report.tools: 可关注Wikipedia Enterprise API、CC BY-SA许可与署名检查工具、robots.txt与速率限制实践，以及带来源元数据和引用追溯的RAG框架，如LangChain、LlamaIndex的检索与许可管理组件。
